Because the 'vulnerable symbol' is static data rather than code, name-based AST search for 'TrustCor' correctly returns zero matches and cannot determine reachability — the real question is whether CTFd's production code performs outbound HTTPS requests (e.g. via requests/urllib3, which default to certifi's bundle for verification) that an attacker could intercept with a TrustCor-chained certificate. None of the retrieved application snippets (config delete, signing/serialization, admin reset) touch networking or TLS client code, so there is no direct evidence either confirming or ruling out such outbound HTTPS usage. Given certifi is a transitive dependency almost certainly pulled in by an HTTP client library used somewhere in a full web application (e.g., for integrations, notifications, or update checks), but no such call site was surfaced by retrieval, this cannot be confidently resolved from the evidence provided.

reflection.critique: The strongest counter-argument is that this advisory is fundamentally different from a code-reachability question: certifi's 'TrustCor' symbol is bundled PEM data, not an API that application code calls. The AST search for 'TrustCor' or certifi call sites is structurally incapable of ever showing reachability for this class of advisory, so a 'not_reachable' verdict based on zero symbol references would be a false negative (any app using requests/urllib3 with default TLS verification is implicitly 'reachable' to the stale trust store). Conversely, a 'reachable' verdict would also be premature because the advisory's real precondition (an active MITM presenting a certificate chained to the already-untrustworthy TrustCor root) is almost never met and none of the five retrieved snippets show any outbound HTTPS/requests call site in CTFd's own code. The reviewer correctly identifies this tension and refuses to guess in either direction — that is the right call given the evidence provided. One could push toward 'not_reachable' on the grounds that this advisory class is near-universally non-actionable (requires attacker possession of a revoked-trust CA chain plus active network interception), but that is a risk-acceptance argument, not evidence that CTFd lacks outbound TLS usage — and CTFd does perform outbound HTTPS in several places (OAuth/MajorLeagueCyber integration, webhook notifications, SMTP-over-TLS) that weren't surfaced by the retrieval, so 'not_reachable' cannot be asserted confidently either. The uncertain verdict is therefore the most defensible position; it does not ignore or misread the cited evidence.

GHSA-43fp-rhv2-5gv8 (CVE-2022-23491)
package: certifi
summary: Certifi removing TrustCor root certificate
affected: >=2017.11.05, <2022.12.07

GHSA-43fp-rhv2-5gv8 (certifi) details:
Certifi 2022.12.07 removes root certificates from "TrustCor" from the root store. These are in the process of being removed from Mozilla's trust store.

TrustCor's root certificates are being removed pursuant to an investigation prompted by media reporting that TrustCor's ownership also operated a business that produced spyware. Conclusions of Mozilla's investigation can be found [here](https://groups.google.com/a/mozilla.org/g/dev-security-policy/c/oxX69KFvsm4/m/yLohoVqtCgAJ).

GHSA-248v-346w-9cwc (CVE-2024-39689)
package: certifi
summary: Certifi removes GLOBALTRUST root certificate
affected: >=2021.5.30, <2024.7.4

GHSA-248v-346w-9cwc (certifi) details:
Certifi 2024.07.04 removes root certificates from "GLOBALTRUST" from the root store. These are in the process of being removed from Mozilla's trust store.

GLOBALTRUST's root certificates are being removed pursuant to an investigation which identified "long-running and unresolved compliance issues". Conclusions of Mozilla's investigation can be found [here]( https://groups.google.com/a/mozilla.org/g/dev-security-policy/c/XpknYMPO8dI).
